messages.content:
Work out the ICD-10-AM principal diagnosis category for the episode below. The principal diagnosis is the single condition established after investigation to be chiefly responsible for the patient's episode of admitted care. It is not the patient's most serious comorbidity, not the presenting symptom, and not the procedure performed.

Think in three steps: first name the condition chiefly responsible for the admission, second name the ICD-10-AM chapter letter it belongs to, third give the three-character category.

Example 1
Hospital course: A 72-year-old man with a 50 pack-year smoking history was admitted with three days of worsening breathlessness and purulent sputum. Spirometry showed an FEV1/FVC ratio of 0.52. He was treated with nebulised bronchodilators, oral prednisolone and antibiotics for an infective exacerbation of his long-standing airflow limitation.
Answer: Irreversible airflow limitation in a heavy smoker with an infective exacerbation is chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, chapter J, category J44.
CODE: J44

Example 2
Hospital course: A 58-year-old man presented with crushing central chest pain radiating to the jaw. The electrocardiogram showed ST elevation in the anterior leads and high-sensitivity troponin rose from 40 to 2100 ng/L. He underwent primary percutaneous coronary intervention with a stent to the proximal left anterior descending artery.
Answer: ST elevation with a rising troponin and culprit-vessel stenting is an acute myocardial infarction, chapter I, category I21.
CODE: I21

Hospital course:
Discharge Summary:
 
Patient Name: [Redacted] 
Date of Admission: [Redacted] 
Date of Discharge: [Redacted] 
Admitting Diagnosis: [diagnosis section withheld]
Summary:
A 59-year-old male patient was admitted to our hospital with a high PSA level of 218.5 ng/mL and was diagnosed with adenocarcinoma of the prostate with a Gleason score of 4＋5. Further testing revealed bone metastases of the right rib and L2 vertebra, with a clinical stage of T2aN0M1. The patient was treated with radiation therapy and androgen deprivation therapy (ADT), and his PSA level dropped to 0.053 ng/mL. At the age of 56 years, his PSA level was again elevated, and he was restarted on different hormonal treatments with flutamide, estramustine phosphate, enzalutamide, and abiraterone. At the age of 58 years, the patient developed a resistance to hormonal therapies.  
 
Using 11C-choline PET/CT imaging, multiple bone metastases without lymph node metastases or visceral metastases were confirmed. The patient then completed six cycles of Ra-223 therapy without any interruption and adverse effects. The third 11C-choline PET/CT after six cycles showed that existing lesions increased and new uptake spots were found in the thoracic spine, sacrum, right rib, and right ileum. During Ra-223 therapy, the patient’s serum ALP did not dramatically change, but PSA levels gradually increased. After the completion of Ra-223 therapy, a new chemotherapy with cabazitaxel was started.  

At the time of discharge, the patient’s symptoms and biochemical progression remained. Close monitoring, continuation of therapies, and further treatment are recommended. The patient should continue follow-ups with his primary care physician.

Write your reasoning in at most three short sentences, then a final line of exactly 'CODE: <letter><digit><digit>'.

text:
Castration-resistant prostate adenocarcinoma with progressive bone metastases is the condition chiefly responsible for this episode, treated with Ra-223 and then cabazitaxel. Cabazitaxel is systemic therapy directed at the primary cancer, so I chose the primary rather than the bone metastases (C79.5), which Ra-223 specifically targets. Malignant neoplasm of the prostate is in chapter C, category C61.

CODE: C61
